g.text: Large language models encode extensive factual knowledge in their
parameters, but this knowledge can become outdated or incorrect after
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Large language models encode extensive factual knowledge in their parameters, but this knowledge can become outdated or incorrect after deployment.

g.text: Model editing (Wang et al., 2023b) aims to update specific factual
associations without full retraining, enabling efficient knowledge
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=1) Model editing (Wang et al., 2023b) aims to update specific factual associations without full retraining, enabling efficient knowledge maintenance.

g.text: Methods such as ROME (Meng et al., 2022a), MEMIT (Meng et al.,
2022b), and localized fine-tuning (Yang et al., 2025b) have
demonstrated success in modifying model outputs for targeted
g.title: N3 [Prior_Work] (cites=3) Methods such as ROME (Meng et al., 2022a), MEMIT (Meng et al., 2022b), and localized fine-tuning (Yang et al., 2025b) have demonstrated success in modifying model outputs for targeted prompts while preserving general capabilities.

g.text: However, current editing methods focus primarily on token-level
generation accuracy—whether the model produces the correct new
g.title: N4 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, current editing methods focus primarily on token-level generation accuracy—whether the model produces the correct new answer when prompted.

g.text: Edited models can't judge truth of edits
Recent work has revealed a critical gap: edited models often
cannot reliably judge the truth of statements containing their own
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=1) Recent work has revealed a critical gap: edited models often cannot reliably judge the truth of statements containing their own edited facts (Liu et al., 2025).

g.text: Example: gen 'English' but can't judge true
For example, a model edited to associate "Danielle Darrieux" with "English"
as her mother language may correctly generate "English" when prompted, yet
fail to judge "The mother language of Danielle Darrieux is English" as true.
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) For example, a model edited to associate "Danielle Darrieux" with "English" as her mother language may correctly generate "English" when prompted, yet fail to judge "The mother language of Danielle Darrieux is English" as true.

g.text: This semantic inconsistency undermines the trustworthiness of edits as
g.title: N7 [Limitation] (cites=0) This semantic inconsistency undermines the trustworthiness of edits as genuine knowledge updates.

g.text: A natural approach is to add truth-judgment supervision during
g.title: N8 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) A natural approach is to add truth-judgment supervision during editing.

g.text: However, simply training the model to output "True" for edited
facts is insufficient—the model can learn an "always True"
shortcut, achieving perfect accuracy on positive examples while
g.title: N9 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, simply training the model to output "True" for edited facts is insufficient—the model can learn an "always True" shortcut, achieving perfect accuracy on positive examples while failing on negative ones.

g.text: This yields chance-level performance on balanced evaluation.
g.title: N10 [Limitation] (cites=0) This yields chance-level performance on balanced evaluation.

g.text: We propose Fact-Check Grounding (FCG), which adds balanced truth-conditional
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) We propose Fact-Check Grounding (FCG), which adds balanced truth-conditional supervision during editing.

g.text: For each edit, FCG trains the model to judge the new fact as "True" and the
old fact as "False", forcing genuine truth discrimination rather than
g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=0) For each edit, FCG trains the model to judge the new fact as "True" and the old fact as "False", forcing genuine truth discrimination rather than format-based shortcuts.

g.text: C1: propose FCG with balanced T/F
We propose FCG, a method that augments model editing with balanced
True/False supervision to improve semantic consistency.
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We propose FCG, a method that augments model editing with balanced True/False supervision to improve semantic consistency.

g.text: We demonstrate that FCG improves balanced fact-check accuracy
(BFC-Acc) by +12.3 points over the LocFT-BF baseline (p = 0.0044)
on KnowEdit ZsRE, while the format-only control achieves only
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We demonstrate that FCG improves balanced fact-check accuracy (BFC-Acc) by +12.3 points over the LocFT-BF baseline (p = 0.0044) on KnowEdit ZsRE, while the format-only control achieves only chance-level performance.

g.text: We reveal an important limitation: FCG's improvement is
template-specific, with limited transfer to paraphrased prompts
(+2.44 points, not significant), indicating that the model learns
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We reveal an important limitation: FCG's improvement is template-specific, with limited transfer to paraphrased prompts (+2.44 points, not significant), indicating that the model learns template-label associations rather than semantically robust truth-judgment.
